blocks.text: I can identify the correct spelling of a homophone based on its context.

items.title: {homophones}
items.sub: words that sound the same

items.title: {noun or verb?}
items.sub: -ce and -se endings

items.title: temperature and aggressive
items.sub: two curriculum words

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: Words that sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings.
The different types of words that are used to form sentences. Adjectives, nouns, verbs and adverbs are examples of word class.
The surrounding words or sentences that help determine the meaning of a word or phrase.

blocks.text: Homophone comes from Greek: ‘homos’ means ‘one and the same’ and ‘phon’ means ‘sound’, so it means ‘same sound’. Look at these two sentences.

items: Walk to the end of the road and turn {right} after the traffic lights.
When we move house, you could {write} to your friends regularly.

items.title: {right}
items.sub: r-i-g-h-t

items.title: {write}
items.sub: the act of writing with a pen or pencil. The w is silent.

blocks.text: They sound exactly alike, but they are spelt differently and have different meanings. If we switched them around, the sentences would not make sense.
Homophones can belong to different word classes. Knowing their meaning helps us to understand and spell them.

items.title: {sell}
items.sub: a verb: exchanging something for money. They sell fresh vegetables in the market.

items.title: {cell}
items.sub: a noun: a very small room. The prisoner’s cell was grim and bare.

blocks.label: ‘Cell’ has other meanings too!
blocks.text: Cell is also a homonym. All living things are made of cells, the small parts that make up a living thing. Cells are also found in spreadsheets that we use on a computer. Use the context to work out which meaning it is.

blocks.q: Use the context to choose the correct spelling.

items.q: The prisoner was locked in his ___.
A ___ is a tiny part that makes up a living thing.
I am going to ___ my old toys at the market.

blocks.text: These two sound exactly the same. The difference is -ce or -se at the end.

items.title: practi{ce}
items.sub: a noun, a place: The dental practice is always busy.

items.title: practi{se}
items.sub: a verb, an action: You must practise your spellings before the test next week.

blocks.text: The noun ends in {-ce} and the verb ends in {-se}.
The same pattern works for licence and license. Just like practice and practise, the noun ends in -ce and the verb ends in -se.

items.title: licen{ce}
items.sub: a noun: a thing you need to have. You need to be 17 before you can get a driving licence.

items.title: licen{se}
items.sub: a verb, a doing word. They will need to license the shop before it can sell anything.

blocks.text: Here the noun and the verb differ at the end again: -cy for the noun, -sy for the verb.

items.title: prophe{cy}
items.sub: a noun: a prediction of what will happen. The ancient book foretold a prophecy about a hero.

items.title: prophe{sy}
items.sub: a verb: the act of making the prediction. She could prophesy about future events.

blocks.label: How can knowing the word class help?
blocks.text: Knowing the word class of a word in a sentence can sometimes help us to spell it correctly. With these word pairs, if you need a noun (a thing), use -ce or -cy. If you need a verb (a doing word), use -se or -sy.

blocks.q: Use the spelling of each word to work out its word class.
Decide if you need a noun or a verb, then choose.

items.q: The dentist’s ___ is opposite the park.
I need to ___ my spellings every night.
You need a ___ to drive a car.
The council will ___ the new shop.
The wise woman could ___ what would happen.

blocks.text: Three words, one sound. Look at the letters that are different.

items.title: {sc}ent
items.sub: a smell

items.title: {s}ent
items.sub: I sent something by post.

items.title: {c}ent
items.sub: a unit of money. I bought it for 10 cents.

items.q: The ___ of the roses filled the room.
Yesterday I ___ a card to my gran.

blocks.text: There are no patterns for homophones, so we come up with our own ideas to help us remember.

items.title: ta{il} or ta{le}?
items.sub: A tail is the last part of an animal, and ‘tail’ ends in l for last. A tale often finishes with ‘The End’, and ‘tale’ ends in e.

items.title: c{e}real
items.sub: The c looks like a bowl on its side. The e instead of i can be something we eat early in the morning.

items.title: s{e}rial
items.sub: A serial is part of a series, like a television serial. The word serial links to series.

blocks.text: Every morning, I have a bowl of cereal for breakfast. What is your favourite television serial to watch? A tale is a traditional folk tale.
Spelling rules help, but we also need to practise. Practising helps you remember words more easily, notice how they are spelt and feel more confident.

items: **Look** carefully at the word. Pay attention to any tricky parts.
**Copy** the word. Write the tricky part larger. You could even draw a ‘naughty’ face on the letter.

blocks.q: Which is the correct order for the naughty letters strategy?
options: Copy with a naughty letter, then look carefully
Look carefully, then copy with a naughty letter
blocks.why: We should always look carefully at spellings before we practise them.

blocks.q: Look, cover, write, check. Make the tricky part big!

blocks.text: Now for two words to learn by heart.

items.title: temp{e}rature
items.sub: The temperature outside is very warm.

items.title: a{gg}re{ss}ive
items.sub: She played the game aggressively.

items: **temperature**: the vowel in the middle is unstressed, so it is easy to forget or misspell. Watch out for that ‘e’. The -ture at the end makes a ch sound.
**aggressive**: the double g and double s can be mistaken for single letters. It also has a silent ‘e’ at the end.

blocks.q: Which of these is spelt correctly?

items: Two or more words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings are called **homophones**.
Licence and license, practice and practise, and prophecy and prophesy are homophones. In these pairs the noun ends -ce (or -cy) and the verb ends -se (or -sy).
We can look for **naughty letters** to help us remember tricky spellings.

flashcards.back:
Words that sound the same, but have different spellings and meanings.

Example: right / write.

sell (verb): to exchange something for money.
cell (noun): a very small room. Cells are also the small parts that make up living things.

flashcards.front: Is ‘practice’ (-ce) a noun or a verb? And ‘practise’ (-se)?
flashcards.back:
practice (-ce) is the noun: The dental practice is always busy.
practise (-se) is the verb: Practise your spellings.

flashcards.front: Which spelling do you use for the thing you need to drive a car: licence or license?
flashcards.back: licence (-ce), the noun. The verb is license (-se): to license a shop.

flashcards.front: Which spelling is the noun: prophecy or prophesy?
flashcards.back:
prophecy (-cy) is the noun: a prediction.
prophesy (-sy) is the verb: making the prediction.

flashcards.front: What pattern helps with practice/practise, licence/license and prophecy/prophesy?
flashcards.back: The noun has a c (-ce or -cy) and the verb has an s (-se or -sy).

flashcards.front: What do scent, sent and cent mean?
flashcards.back:
scent: a smell.
sent: as in ‘I sent something by post’.
cent: a unit of money.

flashcards.front: How can you remember tail and tale?
flashcards.back:
tail ends in l for last: the last part of an animal.
tale ends in e for end: a tale often finishes with ‘The End’.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between ‘cereal’ and ‘serial’?
flashcards.back:
cereal: the food you eat for breakfast.
serial: part of a series, like a television serial.

flashcards.front: How can you remember the c and e in ‘cereal’?
flashcards.back: The c looks like a bowl on its side. The e (not i) can be remembered as something we eat early in the morning.

flashcards.front: Is there a spelling rule for homophones?
flashcards.back: No. We must learn them by sight and use practice strategies, like naughty letters, to help us remember.

flashcards.front: What is the naughty letters strategy?
flashcards.back: Look carefully at the word, then copy it with the tricky part written larger (you could draw a naughty face).

flashcards.front: What is tricky about the spelling of ‘temperature’?
flashcards.back: The vowel in the middle is unstressed, so it is easy to forget the ‘e’. The -ture at the end makes a ch sound.

flashcards.front: What is tricky about the spelling of ‘aggressive’?
flashcards.back: It has a double g and a double s, and a silent ‘e’ at the end.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Spelling more homophones
worksheet.instructions: Use the context and the word class (noun or verb) to choose the correct homophone. Type your answer as a single word.

questions.prompt: Before driving a car, you need a ___ to show you are capable. (A noun. Choose licence or license.)
questions.explanation: We need a noun here, and the noun ends in -ce.

questions.prompt: The prisoner shared his ___ with one other person. (Choose sell or cell.)
questions.explanation: Here it is a noun: a very small room.

questions.prompt: I will ___ the piano for an hour after school. (A verb. Choose practice or practise.)
questions.explanation: It is something you do, a verb, so it ends in -se.

questions.prompt: As a hobby, I like to buy and ___ stamps. (Choose sell or cell.)
questions.explanation: It is a verb, a doing word: to exchange something for money.

questions.prompt: They lived in fear that the ___ would come true. (A noun. Choose prophecy or prophesy.)
questions.explanation: A prophecy is a noun, a prediction, and it ends in -cy.

questions.prompt: Which homophone of ‘right’ means to put words on paper with a pen or pencil? (The w is silent.)
questions.explanation: Write is the act of writing with a pen or pencil.

questions.prompt: The ___ of freshly baked bread filled the kitchen. (Choose the word that means a smell: scent, sent or cent.)
Which spelling means a traditional folk tale: tail or tale?
questions.explanation: Tale ends in e for end. Tail ends in l for last.

questions.prompt: Each morning, I have a bowl of ___ for breakfast. (Choose cereal or serial.)
questions.explanation: Cereal is the food you eat. A serial is part of a series.

questions.prompt: The ___ outside is very warm. (Spell the curriculum word for how hot or cold it is.)
questions.explanation: temperature: watch out for the unstressed ‘e’ in the middle.

questions.prompt: How many letter g’s are in the word ‘aggressive’? Write the number.
questions.explanation: Aggressive has a double g and a double s: a-g-g-r-e-s-s-i-v-e.
